title: Daol Securities lifts GS E&C target as Korea data center orders surge - CHOSUNBIZ - Chosunbiz
content: Daol Investment & Securities said on the 1st that orders for data center projects are moving into full swing for GS Engineering & Construction(33,450 won ▼ 500 -1.47%). It kept its "buy (BUY)" recommendation and raised its target price to 48,000 won from 38,000 won. The previous trading day's closing price of GS Engineering & Construction was 33,950 won. Park Young-do, an analyst at Daol Investment & Securities, said, "Revenue recognition from the data center order backlog will begin in earnest in 2026," and noted, "The data center pipeline on a consolidation basis, including XIC&A, will be recognized sequentially as revenue from 2027 to 2029." GS Engineering & Construction has won data center construction contracts including Naver Data Center phases 2 and 3 and LG Uplus Paju1239, and these projects are scheduled to enter the process starting in 2026. Park projected, "Because data centers concentrate mechanical, electrical and plumbing (MEP) work after the structural frame is completed, revenue typically ramps up from the second year after groundbreaking, so contributions to results will expand in 2027–2028." Park added, "Back-to-back orders are continuing from the same clients, including the LG Uplus Pyeongchon Megacenter, NextIDC and Paju1239," and said, "Because data centers are assets premised on uninterruptible operation, existing execution records will serve as a competitive edge for additional orders." Group-level AI infrastructure investment at GS Group is also a factor raising expectations for additional orders. GS Engineering & Construction established "GS AI Infrastructure" in June and combined the capabilities of affiliates including GS Engineering & Construction, GS EPS, GS E&R (power generation) and GS Caltex (cooling). Because the group can procure power and cooling infrastructure together in-house, it is seen as advantageous in meeting the power usage effectiveness (PUE) standards required by data center clients. Park said, "If the Donghae AI data center campus being promoted by GS Group takes concrete shape, the scale of data center orders could expand further," and added, "Along with an improving housing market, the data center business is expected to quickly fill the future revenue gap." title: RU Shibir cancelled Rucsu GS Ammar's 'Sathi' membership last year, expelled over allegations of post trading - The Business Standard
content: Rajshahi University Central Students' Union (Rucsu) General Secretary Salahuddin Ammar was a "Sathi" of Bangladesh Islami Chhatra Shibir and had his status cancelled last year after failing to adequately respond to allegations including financial irregularities and the trading of positions in the metropolitan Chhatra Shakti unit. According to a letter issued by RU Shibir unit on 31 July, Shibir's monthly secretariat meeting in February 2025 decided to suspend Ammar's "Sathi" membership over allegations of moral misconduct, neglect of basic religious duties, freely mixing with women, illegal financial transactions and involvement in activities contrary to the organisation's aims and objectives. The letter said the September 2025 monthly secretariat meeting later decided to cancel his "Sathi" membership after he failed to adequately respond to the allegations. The letter also expressed concern that Ammar's activities and alleged involvement in "criminal activities" could create instability on campus. It said his "provocative activities" could also push the university towards conflict. Signed by Shibir's RU unit President Mujahid Faisal, the letter instructed Shibir leaders to stop communicating with Ammar. It also instructed activists to avoid Ammar in their online and offline activities and refrain from making any negative comments or reactions about him. It also urged elected Rucsu office-bearers not to maintain organisational ties with Ammar and asked Shibir activists at all levels to sever contact with him. Ahmed Munshi, sports secretary of the unit's 2025 committee, and two other leaders of its current committee confirmed the authenticity of the letter to The Business Standard today (30 September). A Shibir leader, speaking on condition of anonymity, said an investigation committee had been formed to look into various allegations against Ammar, including the theft of laptops from a city corporation building, trading in positions in the metropolitan Chhatra Shakti unit and financial irregularities. Asked about Ammar's political background, the leader said Ammar had originally been a "Sathi" of Shibir's Tamirul Millat Madrasah unit and worked with Alternative Literature - a cultural organisation at Rajshahi University. The leader claimed that the organisation was primarily run by Shibir members and that Ammar had been formally involved with Shibir until after the July Uprising in 2024. Another Shibir leader, also speaking on condition of anonymity, said the organisation initially suspended Ammar's membership under its rules and sought his response to the allegations. The decision to cancel his membership was taken after he failed to adequately respond, the leader said. The latest letter was issued after further alleged irregularities were observed and amid concerns over Ammar's conduct, the leader added. Previously, Ammar has repeatedly denied having any affiliation with Shibir. He was elected Rucsu general secretary from the "Anti-Dominance Unity" panel, which was widely discussed as a "dummy panel" of Shibir during the 2025 Rucsu election. He later drew controversy over several campus incidents, including multiple mob incidents, alleged irregularities in financial transactions involving Rucsu funds and incidents in which students were beaten. During that time, Shibir's RU unit said at a press conference that it would not take responsibility for Ammar. This reporter made several attempts to contact Ammar for comment, but received no response. Rajshahi University Central Students’ Union (Rucsu) General Secretary Salahuddin Ammar has lost his "Sathi" membership of Islami Chhatra Shibir over allegations of moral misconduct and violation of organisational discipline. Rajshahi University unit Chhatra Shibir General Secretary Hafez Mehedi Hasan confirmed the development to The Daily Star. “The matter dates back to 2025. He [Salahuddin Ammar] was expelled from the organisation over allegations of irregularities,” he said. Mehedi also said Ammar’s "Sathi" membership was first suspended on February 2, 2025, and he was given an opportunity to defend himself. As he failed to do so, he was expelled from the organisation in September that year, he said. According to the party, "Sathi" is a stage in becoming a full member of Islami Chhatra Shibir. After completing this stage, a person can become a member and hold a position in the organisation. Although Ammar’s "Sathi" membership was cancelled on July 31 this year in a letter signed by Rajshahi University unit Shibir President Mujahid Faisal, the decision only came to light recently. According to the letter, Ammar’s "Sathi" membership was initially suspended at the RU unit Shibir’s monthly secretariat meeting in February 2025 over allegations of ethical misconduct, negligence in performing basic religious obligations, inappropriate association with women, illegal financial transactions and misappropriation of assets, and involvement in activities contrary to the organisation’s aims and objectives. The letter said Ammar failed to provide a satisfactory explanation in response to the allegations. Subsequently, the monthly secretariat meeting in September 2025 decided to cancel his "Sathi" membership. It also said the organisation believed Ammar’s activities, including his alleged involvement in criminal offences in some cases, were creating instability on campus. Shibir leaders and activists were instructed not to make any positive or negative comments or reactions about his online or offline activities, according to the letter. Only elected Rucsu office-bearers were allowed to maintain official communication with him, the letter added. Ammar was elected Rucsu GS in the 2025 election from the “Adhipotto-Birodhi Oikya” panel. The panel was widely described at the time as a “dummy panel” of Shibir. When contacted on Wednesday night, Salahuddin Ammar said in a WhatsApp message that he was attending a Rucsu session but did not comment about the allegations. He later denied the allegations in a Facebook post. “I have been accused of having inappropriate relationships with women, extortion and selling posts in exchange for money. I want to make it clear that I have no involvement in any of these allegations. If someone makes an allegation, there should also be evidence to support it. More importantly, how can I be expected to prove that I did not do something?” he said. “I urge those who have made these allegations to make their evidence public. I am ready to clarify the matter through my statements and record of work,” he added. Ammar also said, “I hope that from today onwards, no one will insult me by calling me a Shibir.” Copyright: Any unauthorized use or reproduction of The Daily Star content for commercial purposes

title: Blazo Gjorev and Panteleon GS Co-Host BCIU Business Roundtable at The Yale Club in New York - The Manila Times
content: Macedonian entrepreneur brings his country's business closer to the American market at The Yale Club during UN General Assembly week NEW YORK, Sept. 30, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Blazo Gjorev, a Macedonian entrepreneur who leads Gjorev Holding, a group of companies operating across the United States and North Macedonia, co-hosted a high-level business roundtable in New York together with the Business Council for International Understanding (BCIU). Held at the prestigious Yale Club during the week of the United Nations General Assembly, the event brought together senior American business leaders and a high-level Macedonian delegation for a direct conversation on strengthening ties between the two markets. By co-hosting the roundtable through Panteleon GS, Blazo Gjorev created a rare setting where the top of the American business community and partners from a smaller market meet directly, in one room. Founded in 1955 as an initiative of the White House under President Dwight D. Eisenhower, BCIU is a nonpartisan organization of more than 200 leading companies, and one of the few forums where global business leaders convene at the highest level, which makes the co-hosting role of a Macedonian company all the more notable. The role reflects more than two decades of Gjorev's work connecting the American and Macedonian markets, with operations on both sides of the Atlantic. "Being part of a conversation at this level is a privilege, not only for our companies, but for Macedonian business as a whole," said Blazo Gjorev. "Connections between these two markets are built over years, not overnight. I intend to keep building them, and to gladly share what I have learned with other Macedonian companies ready to make the same journey." Panteleon GS, based in Skopje, specializes in business-process outsourcing for companies operating in the U.S. market, with a focus on the transportation and logistics industry, providing support in finance, accounting, factoring, leasing, insurance, and controlling. It enables Macedonian professionals to build international careers from home while serving American companies. Gjorev Holding is a private group of companies with a presence on both sides of the Atlantic, active in finance, mobility, logistics, construction, and operational services, bringing together several independent companies across the United States and North Macedonia under a shared strategic direction. title: The Lexus Sedan That Can Make A Used BMW 5 Series Look Risky - Top Speed
content: Subscribe to the TopSpeed newsletter to never miss an update Lexus is Toyota's luxury brand, so it isn't surprising that its mother company's reputation for reliability carries over. The first-generation Lexus LS was built with reliability in mind—so much so, that even how the leather, exterior trim, and other bits and pieces of the vehicle age was considered. This is peak Lexus, when nothing was shared with mainstream Toyota siblings, as the first-generation LS was built on its own platform and barely shared any parts with a Toyota. Today, while most Lexus models are based on Toyota platforms, there are some models that stand out. One such model is the used Lexus sedan for today's article. This Lexus is severely underrated, in my opinion, and when it came out, I even preferred it to the equivalent BMW 5 Series of its time. While it didn't get enough attention as I would have liked, today this Lexus luxury sedan is finally in the spotlight among used car buyers. Not only is today's Lexus luxury sedan more reliable than the BMW 5 Series, but its rarity adds a sense of novelty to its existence in 2026. Today's Lexus sedan has never caught up with the BMW 5 Series in terms of sales, so what makes the 5 Series the segment's primary choice, even versus its other German rivals? A vehicle that stands out is often one whose driving dynamics also stand out. The BMW 5 Series easily stood out among its peers, whether German or otherwise, for its athletic driving dynamics. I wouldn't outright say the word "sporty" because, if I were being honest, the 5 Series had varying degrees of sportiness across various generations, with this new one having somewhat numb steering, as I've already driven the current G60 and the previous G30 as well. Nevertheless, all 5 Series generations were athletic next to their comfort-oriented rivals. Yet, at the same time, the 5 Series didn't compromise too much on comfort. Sure, older 5 Series generations had a stiffer suspension, but they were never considered uncomfortable for luxury sedan duty. Today, the 5 Series has gotten so comfortable that it's more like a scaled-down 7 Series now instead of being a bigger 3 Series, and by having a degree of athleticism, it's enough for its driving dynamics to stand out. Luxury sells heavily on emotion, and BMW's marketing tagline of "The Ultimate Driving Machine" resonates extremely well with luxury buyers. Mercedes-Benz is a brand primarily known for comfort and prestige, which is why it's defined by the S-Class, as opposed to BMW, whose brand identity is centered around its sportier, more agile models like the 3 Series and 5 Series. Unlike the full-size luxury sedan segment, where luxury and comfort become top priority, the midsize segment still has buyers looking for something that's sporty and more entertaining to drive. That's the reason why there have only been a handful of full-size luxury sedans with performance intent, namely the V-12-powered Mercedes-Benz S 65 AMG and the BMW M760Li, both of which only lasted for one generation. Meanwhile, the compact and midsize luxury sedan segments have a ton of high-performance offerings from Germany, the UK, America, and at one point, even Japan. Speaking of which, the market value of the high-performance variant of the Lexus sedan in today's article is starting to rise, reflecting how enthusiasts are finally recognizing its worthiness and how it was severely underrated when it was still sold. And with that, the used Lexus sedan I would choose in a heartbeat over a BMW 5 Series is the GS—particularly the final fourth-generation model (codenamed L10). Here's why. Development of the fourth-generation Lexus GS began as far back as 2007, with its design being finalized around 2009, with then CEO Akio Toyoda steering the development of the GS into his desired direction. That's because the GS was the centerpiece of Akio Toyoda's vision to imbue a sense of passion into the Lexus brand. And indeed, they chose the perfect vehicle to become the brand's centerpiece for its new, edgier image. The GS is rear-wheel drive (RWD), and was styled with sportiness and distinction in mind. The L-Finesse design evolved to feature the now-iconic Spindle Grille, which, though controversial, was a far cry from the simpler, more straightforward designs of every Lexus before it. The GS was so different from any Lexus or Toyota model before it that it ditched the Japanese-market Crown's N platform for the New N platform, and this platform was eventually inherited by the IS and RC. The fourth-generation Lexus GS was sold in two versions in the United States—a GS 350 in both all-wheel drive (AWD) and RWD and the rarer GS 450h performance hybrid. Both models got a 3.5-liter V-6, specifically, the ever-reliable 2GR-FSE or 2GR-FKS from 2015 onwards, or the hybrid-specific 2GR-FXS. These engines have been developed with performance and refinement in mind. These engines also feature D-4S direct and port injection, eliminating the carbon buildup of direct injection since the engine reverts to port injection under light loads. A six-speed automatic was the standard transmission, but the RWD model got a newer eight-speed automatic in 2014. Opting for the F Sport also adds rear-wheel steering, which helps its handling agility, as well as Adaptive Variable Suspension. Critics immediately praised the GS 350 for being a tidy handler—one that truly offered a sporty and thrilling driving experience never before seen from the brand. It is also reliable, with the GR V-6 engines already proven today to last extremely long. iSeeCars says that the GS 350 has an average lifespan of 165,888 miles, or about 15.4 years. With a 30.3 percent chance of lasting at least 200,000 miles, the GS is one of the longest-lasting cars you can buy. For reference, the BMW 5 Series has an average lifespan of 109,383 miles, or 10.2 years, and a minuscule 2.2 percent chance of reaching at least 200,000 miles. Data for the GS 450h, however, is a bit harder to find, especially since the hybrid version wasn't sold in high numbers. Unfortunately, the fourth-generation Lexus GS ended production in 2020 with no successor ever planned. The ES is your only choice for a midsize luxury sedan from Lexus, but I think we can all agree that it just isn't the same, nor as special, as the GS. The BMW 5 Series handily outsold the Lexus GS, and with so much supply in the used market, the GS has a far higher resale value today than its German counterpart. The GS was sold from the 2012 to 2020 model years, and when compared to the two BMW 5 Series generations of its time, its German rival may have the technology and slight sportiness edge. While the GS didn't necessarily push the boundaries of tech, the mere fact that it had a distinct design while meeting the expectations of those wanting a sports luxury midsize sedan makes this a severely underrated option. If you want a used GS 350, Kelley Blue Book says that a final 2020 model year Lexus GS has an average value of $24,300, which is much higher than the $18,050 average value for a 2020 BMW 5 Series. Enthusiasts are finally realizing today just how great the GS sedan is, and this part couldn't be any more true than with its high-performance GS F sibling. But if you want something that has a chance of becoming a collector's item in the future, then look no further than the Lexus GS F. This vehicle, in my opinion, is one of the most misunderstood high-performance midsize luxury sedans. It gets a naturally-aspirated 5.0-liter V-8 that pumps out 467 horsepower and 389 pound-feet of torque that's sent through a Torque Vectoring Differential (TVD). These numbers are considerably lower than the BMW M5's more than 500 horsepower with its twin-turbo V-8, but what it lacked in straight-line speed was more than made up for by its sheer character. The V-8 sounded glorious, especially since it was naturally aspirated. Its handling may not be as sharp as an M5's, but it was sharp enough to be entertaining on the road and on track. Since you had to make the 5.0-liter V-8 work harder, it was more satisfying to accelerate with, as power delivery was linear and not brutal enough to bring you to illegal speeds. Of course, it was also reliable—being the UR V-8 engine, it's one of the most reliable engines, period. Today, a used Lexus GS F easily sells for more than $50,000, exceeding the $44,000 average resale value Kelley Blue Book has determined. Meanwhile, the BMW M5 had a much higher starting price than the Lexus GS F, yet its average resale value of $40,100 is the same or even lower than what the GS F commands today. title: GS E&C completes land-based salmon farming trial - koreaherald.com
content:
Business GS E&C completes land-based salmon farming trial Busan facility reuses up to 99% of farming water, with full-scale shipments set to begin this year GS Engineering & Construction has completed a trial of its land-based Atlantic salmon farming operation, using its water treatment technology to build expertise for future aquaculture projects. Its subsidiary Eco Aquafarm marked the milestone with a ceremony at the Busan Smart Aquaculture Cluster in Gijang County on Wednesday. GS E&C CEO Huh Yoon-hong attended alongside officials from the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries and the Busan Metropolitan Government. Eco Aquafarm has managed the full production cycle, from hatching fertilized eggs to raising and shipping salmon. The facility combines a recirculating aquaculture system with digital monitoring and Zero Water Concept technology to reuse up to 99 percent of its farming water. Farming Atlantic salmon requires precise control of temperature, salinity and dissolved oxygen as the fish transition between freshwater and seawater. Heat exchangers and precision controls keep water temperatures at 12-16 degrees Celsius during summer, while a central monitoring system tracks water quality and equipment in real time. The company has applied for a patent for an underwater camera system that helps determine when salmon are ready to move to the next growth stage. GS E&C and Eco Aquafarm secured patents for recirculating aquaculture facilities in 2023 and desalination aquaculture facilities in 2025. To strengthen food safety and quality control, Eco Aquafarm completed seafood traceability and HACCP registration last year and obtained antibiotic-free certification for its Atlantic salmon in June. The companies are also working with LG Electronics to improve hygiene at land-based farms and with the National Institute of Fisheries Science on aquatic disease research and preventive vaccines. GS E&C plans to use the technology, operating experience and data gathered in Busan to expand into other land-based aquaculture projects. “We have accumulated the technologies and operational capabilities needed across the entire land-based aquaculture process, from water treatment and fish cultivation to facility operation, by raising Atlantic salmon at the Busan Smart Aquaculture Cluster,” a GS E&C official said. Completed in December 2024, the cluster has an annual production capacity of 500 tons of Atlantic salmon. GS E&C participates as a private-sector operator through Eco Aquafarm, which plans to begin full-scale shipments later this year. title: GS E&C pilots land-based K-salmon farming, validates year-round RAS in Korea - CHOSUNBIZ - Chosunbiz
content: Eco Aquafarm, a subsidiary of GS Engineering & Construction, succeeded in a pilot project to farm Atlantic salmon on land based on water treatment technology. GS Engineering & Construction said on the 30th that it held a "Clean K-salmon shipping declaration ceremony" at the Busan Smart Aquaculture Cluster in Gijang County, Busan. The event was attended by CEO Huh Yoon-hong of GS Engineering & Construction and officials from the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries and Busan City. GS Engineering & Construction selected land-based salmon farming using water treatment technology as a new business and established Eco Aquafarm in 2020. Since then, it has directly operated the entire process from stocking eyed eggs of Atlantic salmon, hatching, fry, smolt, and adult growth, to water quality management and shipping, building related technology and data. The Busan Smart Aquaculture Cluster adopted a recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) based on GS Engineering & Construction's water treatment technology and smart aquaculture technology based on information and communications technology (ICT). Eco Aquafarm succeeded in land-based farming of Atlantic salmon after more than two years of research and pilot testing. They also validated temperature control technology to raise Atlantic salmon, a cold-water species, year-round in Korea. Although the East Sea and coastal water temperatures have recently risen to 25–28 degrees or higher in summer due to high-temperature events, they maintained 12–16 degrees, suitable for salmon growth, using cooling devices and a precise temperature control system. GS Engineering & Construction plans to develop the water treatment, growth management, and facility operation technologies and data secured through this pilot into a technology and operation platform that can be applied to other land-based aquaculture businesses in the future. An official at GS Engineering & Construction said, "By raising actual Atlantic salmon at the Busan Smart Aquaculture Cluster, we built the technologies and operational capabilities needed for the entire land-based aquaculture process, from water treatment to growth management and facility operation," and added, "Based on the technologies and data we have secured, we will continue to enhance the competitiveness of our land-based aquaculture platform." title: GS E&C succeeds in land-based salmon farming demonstration - The Korea Times
content: GS E&C CEO Huh Yoon-hong speaks during a ceremony to mark the successful demonstration of land-based farming of salmon at Busan Smart Aquaculture Cluster in Busan, Wednesday. Courtesy of GS E&C GS E&C has successfully demonstrated land-based farming of Atlantic salmon using its water treatment technologies, securing capabilities that can be applied and expanded to future aquaculture projects. Eco Aquafarm, a subsidiary established by GS E&C for land-based salmon farming, held a ceremony Wednesday to mark the successful completion of the demonstration project and showcased Atlantic salmon raised at Busan Smart Aquaculture Cluster ahead of commercial shipments. GS E&C CEO Huh Yoon-hong and officials from the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries and Busan city government attended the event, and tasted the land-raised salmon and were briefed on the company’s farming technologies. The cluster is a testbed facility capable of producing up to 500 tons of Atlantic salmon annually, with commercial shipments set to begin by the end of this year Eco Aquafarm was established in 2020 to develop a new business leveraging builder GS E&C’s water treatment technologies. Since then, the subsidiary has operated the entire farming process, from incubating Atlantic salmon eggs and raising fish, managing water quality and shipments. Eco Aquafarm's facility at Busan Smart Aquaculture Cluster in Busan / Courtesy of GS E&C Atlantic salmon require cold, clean water, making precise temperature and water quality control essential for stable year-round farming. To meet such conditions, Eco Aquafarm uses Recirculating Aquaculture System based on GS E&C’s water treatment technologies, so that the water can be continuously filtered and reused. The facility also applies Zero Water Concept technology, which enables up to 99 percent of the water to be reused, creating a more sustainable environment for land-based salmon farming. Salmon hatch in freshwater before growing in seawater, requiring the hatching and smolt stages to take place in freshwater while adult salmon are raised in seawater. This requires advanced ICT-based smart farming technologies to precisely control water temperature, salinity, dissolved oxygen levels and quality to maintain optimal growing conditions. Based on its cooling and precision temperature control systems, Eco Aquafarm maintained water temperatures between 12 and 16 degrees Celsius, optimal for raising Salmon, even during the summertime. Its Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition system collected, recorded and analyzed facility data through sensors while automatically adjusting equipment based on real-time water quality monitoring. The technologies developed by GS E&C and Eco Aquafarm resulted in multiple patents. The companies secured patents related to recirculating aquaculture facilities in 2023 and desalination-based aquaculture facilities in 2025. They have also filed a patent for technology that uses underwater cameras to determine when salmon should be transferred to the next stage of their growing environment. “By raising Atlantic salmon at the cluster, we have built technological and operational capabilities across the entire land-based farming process, from water treatment to growth management and facility operations,” a GS E&C official said. “Based on the technologies and data we have accumulated, we will continue to enhance the competitiveness of our land-based aquaculture platform.” Nam Hyun-woo has worked as a staff writer at The Korea Times since 2013, mostly covering business and politics. title: GS Entec to supply 37 monopiles for Taean offshore wind farm - 헤럴드경제
content: Company entered market in 2022, notching successive wins Annual production capacity to expand to 150,000 tons GS Entec, a subsidiary of GS Global, will supply 37 monopiles — the key foundation structures for offshore wind turbines — to the Taean Offshore Wind Farm being developed off the coast of Taean in South Chungcheong Province. The company signed the monopile supply contract Wednesday at the Seoul headquarters of Taean Wind Power Generation Co., the project developer. Under the agreement, GS Entec will begin full-scale manufacturing in July 2027 and complete deliveries in stages by the end of August 2028. Monopiles are the primary substructure of offshore wind turbines, fabricated by welding large steel plates into a cylindrical form to support the turbine and tower. Applicable in water depths of up to roughly 50 meters, monopiles cost less to manufacture and take less time to install than jacket-type foundations, which is why more than 70 percent of offshore wind projects worldwide use them. The waters off Taean are considered well-suited to monopile construction, with shallow depths and thick sediment layers providing favorable ground conditions. The Taean project is being co-developed by Singapore-based Vena Energy, a global renewable energy developer; Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP) of Denmark; and Korea Western Power. The farm will have a total capacity of 504 MW, with construction targeted to begin in 2028 and be completed in 2030. GS Entec entered the monopile business in 2022 through a strategic technology partnership with Sif, the Dutch company that leads the global market. It went on to supply all 64 monopiles for the Yeonggwang Nagwol Offshore Wind project in 2023, and has now secured the Taean contract as well. This month, the company completed a factory scale-up backed by an investment of about 300 billion won ($221 million), lifting annual production capacity more than threefold — from 40,000 tons to 150,000 tons. The Taean offshore wind project will be the first large-scale order to put that expanded capacity to full use.

title: GS Engineering & Construction Demonstrates Land-Based Salmon Farming Success - chosun.com
content: Overcomes high-temperature challenges using proprietary water treatment and ICT-based technology at Busan facility GS Engineering & Construction has successfully demonstrated technology for land-based farming of Atlantic salmon, laying the foundation for future aquaculture business. GS Engineering & Construction announced on the 30th that it held a ‘Clean K-Salmon Shipment Declaration Ceremony’ at the Busan Smart Aquaculture Cluster in Gijang County, Busan. The event was attended by Huh Yoon-hong, CEO of GS Engineering & Construction, representatives from the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, and Busan City officials, among other guests. Earlier, GS Engineering & Construction selected land-based Atlantic salmon farming using its proprietary water treatment technology as a new business initiative and established the subsidiary Eco Aqua Farm in 2020. Since then, it has accumulated technology and operational data by directly managing the entire process of land-based salmon farming—from hatching eggs to rearing fry, smolt, and adult salmon, water quality management, and shipment. Eco Aqua Farm achieved successful land-based salmon farming after two years of research and validation. This was accomplished through a closed recirculating aquaculture system based on GS Engineering & Construction’s water treatment technology and ICT-based smart aquaculture technology. Atlantic salmon inhabit cold, clean waters, making water temperature control and water quality management critical for their growth in South Korea. However, recent climate anomalies have caused prolonged high-water-temperature phenomena, with coastal waters near the East Sea exceeding 25 degrees Celsius during summer. Eco Aqua Farm overcame these climatic limitations by maintaining water temperatures at the optimal 12–16 degrees Celsius for salmon, even during summer heatwaves, using cooling systems and precision temperature control technology. The facility also filters and purifies breeding water, enabling up to 99% reuse, thereby creating a sustainable salmon farming environment. The Busan Smart Aquaculture Cluster began full-scale Atlantic salmon farming in December 2024 upon its final completion. As a testbed facility capable of producing up to 500 tons of Atlantic salmon annually, it is preparing for full-scale shipments by the end of this year. title: Goldman private credit fund defies industry elevated withdrawal trend yet again - KELO-AM
content: Sept 29 (Reuters) – Goldman Sachs’ private credit fund said on Tuesday that investor requests to pull money further slowed down ​in the third-quarter tender offer, with redemption pressure easing ‌across the broader industry. The $18.2 billion GS Credit fund once again outperformed most other private credit players, with investors seeking to pull just 2% of shares in the latest tender offer, compared with 3.2% in the ‌prior ​quarter. Its repurchase requests have remained ⁠below the customary 5% ⁠limit since inception. Meanwhile, withdrawal requests at the biggest non-traded private credit funds have ranged from 10% to over 16% of shares in the third-quarter tender offers unveiled so far. ​Data from Blue Owl funds is expected in the coming days. Rival funds have grappled with elevated redemption requests throughout ⁠2026, driven by concerns about ⁠lending standards and whether software companies that have ​borrowed heavily from direct lenders will weather AI disruption. That said, redemption ​pressure at major funds is showing signs of ‌easing as asset managers clear backlogs of withdrawal requests and investor sentiment rebounds from recent turbulence. A huge chunk of GS Credit investors come from Goldman’s private wealth channels, who have been ⁠long-term investors in the private credit space and can tolerate illiquidity, Reuters has reported. “The concerns around software-related credit quality that dominated ⁠headlines earlier in ‌2026 have begun to moderate. While Q1’s “SaaSpocalypse” narrative ⁠and Q2’s enterprise software spend uncertainty drove ​aggressive ‌spread widening, the Q3 landscape has shifted meaningfully,” ​GS Credit ⁠said. The event took place at the Busan Smart Aquaculture Cluster in Gijang-gun, Busan, and was attended by GS Engineering & Construction CEO Heo Yun-hong, along with officials from the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, the Busan city government and other guests. Attendees sampled Atlantic salmon raised using domestically developed technology and shared insights on cultivation techniques and operational know-how. GS Engineering & Construction established Eco Aqua Farm in 2020, drawing on its proprietary water treatment technology. Since then, the company has managed every stage of the Atlantic salmon life cycle in-house — from eyed-egg stocking and hatching through grow-out, water quality management and harvesting — accumulating data and expertise along the way. The Busan Smart Aquaculture Cluster employs a recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) that continuously filters and purifies water for reuse, alongside a Zero Water Concept (ZWC) technology that recycles up to 99 percent of the water used. Cooling equipment and a precision temperature control system keep the water within the optimal range of 12 to 16 degrees Celsius for salmon growth even during summer heat waves, overcoming the challenge of high water temperatures. Advanced ICT technology has also been introduced to boost operational efficiency. A supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) system collects, analyzes and automatically controls equipment data via sensors, enabling real-time water quality monitoring. The company has also developed and filed a patent for a technology that uses underwater cameras to determine the optimal timing for transferring salmon between tanks. In addition, the facility has obtained antibiotic-free certification, registered with the fisheries traceability management system and received HACCP approval, securing the safety and quality of its production process. Collaborative research on disease prevention vaccine development and hygiene improvement is also underway with external specialists, including LG Electronics and the National Institute of Fisheries Science. The Busan Smart Aquaculture Cluster is a test-bed facility capable of producing up to 500 metric tons of Atlantic salmon per year and is on track to begin full-scale shipments by the end of this year. "By actually raising Atlantic salmon at the Busan Smart Aquaculture Cluster, we have built up the capabilities needed across the entire land aquaculture process — from water treatment to facility operations," a GS Engineering & Construction official said. "We will continue to strengthen the competitiveness of our land aquaculture platform on the basis of the technology and data we have secured." Meanwhile, GS Engineering & Construction recently established a proof-of-concept center to verify the performance and field applicability of construction robots and AI technology before deploying them at actual construction sites.

Classic car news, hand-picked vehicles, and auction coverage. Choose what lands in your inbox. Some cars get parked because they're broken. Others get parked because someone loved them too much to use them up. This 1989 Nissan 300ZX GS clearly falls into the second camp. Currently listed on Hagerty Marketplace, the Bright Blue Metallic coupe shows just 7,700 miles, wears its original-owner story proudly, and still pairs Nissan's smooth VG30E V6 with the five-speed manual that makes a Z31 so much fun to drive. The Z31-generation 300ZX arrived for 1984 and carried the Z-car name through the rest of the decade with sharp, wedge-shaped styling that still looks right today. Pop-up headlights, a hybrid digital/analog gauge cluster, and available T-tops made it feel like a spaceship compared with the Datsuns that came before it. Buyers could choose the turbocharged VG30ET or, as here, the naturally aspirated 3.0-liter VG30E in GS trim. That naturally aspirated setup is a big part of this car's charm. It's simple, durable, and rev-happy, and connecting it to a five-speed manual delivers the kind of engaging, analog experience that has made clean '80s Japanese sports cars one of the hottest corners of the collector market. If you've followed the rising interest in these cars, you may remember the 21K-mile 1984 300ZX 50th Anniversary Edition we covered, and survivors with this few miles are only getting harder to find. The first thing that grabs you is the color. Bright Blue Metallic (paint code 426) is a wonderfully period-correct shade, and it's matched inside by blue leather upholstery for a head-to-toe coordinated look that screams late-'80s cool. Removable glass T-top panels let you bring the sky inside, while factory fog lights, alloy wheels (swapped for a set of chrome wheels here), and that long, low profile finish the package. According to the listing, the car stayed with a single owner before the selling dealer acquired it. A State of New Jersey new car dealer inspection sticker is still on the windshield, which is the kind of small detail that makes a survivor like this so charming. The clean CARFAX shows initial New Jersey registration starting in December 1989, followed by later Florida and New Jersey registration. This GS came nicely optioned for its day, with power windows, locks, and mirrors, cruise control, air conditioning, a leather-trimmed steering wheel, bucket seats, and an AM/FM stereo with a power antenna. Power steering and disc brakes round out the list. Ahead of the sale, the selling dealer, Vantage Auto, gave the car a tune-up that included new spark plugs, an oil change, and a brake fluid flush. It comes with its owner's manual, a clean CARFAX report, and a clean New Jersey title. Paint meter readings and detailed condition photos are included in the listing's extensive gallery of more than 300 images, so bidders can see exactly what they're getting. Z31s were built in big numbers, but finding one that hasn't been modified, raced, or used up is another story, and finding one with fewer than 8,000 miles is rarer still. Bidding stood at $3,000 at the time of writing, with the auction scheduled to end Thursday, October 8, at 3:20 p.m. EDT. The car is located in Moonachie, New Jersey. For fans of the later Z32 cars, we've also featured a 34-years-owned 1990 300ZX Twin Turbo on Hagerty Marketplace and a final-year 1996 300ZX five-speed. But if you want the purest expression of the '80s Z-car formula, a blue-on-blue, T-top, five-speed GS with this kind of history is tough to beat. title: How Family Businesses Should Plan for Generational Success - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. Companies with significant family ownership generate roughly 70% of global economic output and 60% of the world’s jobs. However, only three in 10 survive to a second generation. In this episode of Goldman Sachs Exchanges, FX de Mallmann, chairman of Goldman Sachs EMEA and chairman of Investment Banking, and Tucker York, chairman of global Wealth Management, discuss why succession is so difficult, how enduring enterprises structure governance, and the mindset shift required after a sale or IPO. Allison Nathan: Welcome to Goldman Sachs Exchanges. I'm Allison Nathan. Here's a number that surprised me when I first read it. Companies where a family still holds a significant stake produce 70% of the world's economic output and 60% of its jobs. But only 3 in 10 reach a second generation. And only about 1 in 10 reaches a third. So, why is that? To help me work through that, I'm joined by two people who see opposite ends of this. FX de Mallmann is Chairman of Goldman Sachs EMEA and Chairman of Investment Banking. He also leads the firm's coverage of large family-owned companies and family offices, which means he's on the corporate side of the table: the capital raises, the IPOs, the sales, and the successions. Tucker York chairs our global wealth management business. He's on the other side: the families, their balance sheets, and the next generation once that capital is created. Allison Nathan: Yes, happy to have you both. So, FX, let's just start with some context here on the size and the scope and the impact of family-owned businesses. I gave a few stats to start us off, but maybe provide a bit more color on that for us. FX de Mallmann: The statistics you quoted are those we included in our recently published report on honoring legacy, which are global statistics. We did dig a little bit deeper into some of the statistics and see how they apply to differ around the world. And what we found is that there is an enormous space on family-owned businesses in all major regions. In the US, for instance, there are over 32 million family-owned businesses, which represent over 80% of all businesses. Those account for over 60% of GDP and over 60% of the overall workforce. If you move from the private company world to the public company world, around 35% of the Fortune 500 companies are family-controlled or have a significant family owner, which is a substantial base. As you move to Europe, there are significant industries that have leaders, companies that are leading the industry, that have either family control or significant family shareholder - in luxury goods, in beauty and cosmetics, in shipping, in consumer goods, in retail, in telco, in business services, in industrial, in defense, in numerous other sectors. The size and scale and the success of some of these entrepreneurs has been outstanding. And as you move to Asia, there are countries where you have very large family conglomerates that control many sectors of the economy that are very diversified, not only vertically, but also horizontally. And you see many of those in India, in Korea, and in numerous other Asia countries where the role that these families play is significant to the economy, but also in their ability to create new businesses and innovate in all the fields where they operate. Allison Nathan: Those numbers are actually absolutely staggering. And I don't think most people think about businesses in that way. If we think about the family-owned businesses, how does the fact of them being family-owned affect how they run and how they operate if you're inside the business? FX de Mallmann: Well, in the word family-owned, there is the word owned. And therefore, each of these businesses tend to be owned or partly owned by an individual or a family that, on average, tend to be both invested economically, financially, but also emotionally in the business and very engaged. And so, we find in our interactions with many of these entrepreneurs that they tend to take a very long-term view on their business. They tend to be rigorous stewards of their management team. They tend to be disciplined allocators of capital. And they also tend to be prudent with respect to the decisions they make, including the investment decisions and their use of leverage. And on balance, a statistic that we have access to show that these businesses, when family controlled, on average, tend to outperform non-family-controlled businesses. Allison Nathan: Tucker, let me bring you into the conversation because you're sitting with these families day-to-day. Again, let me ask you a different version of the question. How does the fact that these businesses are family-owned impact the way they invest? Tucker York: I'll take a step back saying that I agree that the numbers are staggering when you think about the family connectivity to business and GDP, etc. It's worth putting that in context. In the history of civilization, it used to be a much higher percentage than that. It's only in the last couple of centuries where we have more of a corporate structure and the scale that comes from that more permanent capital that comes around that, that's led to this. So, these concepts are age-old, is what I would say. What I find with investors is the moment that you start thinking about next generation, how do you invest? How do you think about those things? As distinct from what do I need to do this week, this month, this quarter? It all turns on a long-term orientation. What do I think is going on in the long-term? How do I think about that? And that juxtaposition between those two things is very different for families who are thinking about next generation and what's going to happen beyond me. Have I created something that will go beyond? And that leads you down to make decisions about where do I think this investment that I make today will be 10 years, 20 years from now? As distinct from where do I think this investment made today will be next quarter when some new information comes out, etcetera, and it goes up or down? Allison Nathan: So, much more longer-term perspective coming from these families and how they manage their businesses. Of course, as you just touched on, Tucker, the big issue they all face is the generational transition, which is a very critical moment, you say FX, both for the businesses and for the families. Talk us through why that is such a critical moment. FX de Mallmann: It's a critical moment because it's a moment where the founder has to make a decision on two topics. Topic number one, should his family, typically his children or any other family members, stay involved in the management, typically the running of the business? And if so, in what capacity? And the second decision is how is he or she going to pass on the stock, the ownership of the company from one generation to the next? And what's the organization he set up in order to do that successfully? The statistics you mentioned before that only a third of the businesses pass on to the second generation, about 10% to the third, in our view, is neither good nor bad. It kind of is what it is. What's important is, does the business benefit from that family ownership? Or does the business benefit from having a broader ownership base? We have seen outstanding case studies in both, some businesses with one founder who decided that it absolutely should not stay within the family, diversify the ownership, brought in professional management and the companies scaled to be enormously successful companies. And we've seen other examples where the founder took absolutely the reverse view. And the business actually tremendously benefited in being controlled and typically also managed by the family. The key question in our view on experience is, what's the process around this decision making? How early in advance is this considered? And what are the mechanisms to make sure the right judgments are exercised, both on the ability of the family to continue to manage and on how to best organize the ownership and make sure the ownership structure and governance survive the passage of time? Allison Nathan: And Tucker, this ultimately all comes down to succession plans. But you found that only about half of the businesses, family businesses, actually have succession plans, but mostly informal. And only about a third actually write down these plans. So, why is it so hard when this is so critical to their future? Tucker York: I think business succession, like all businesses, go through that and the businesses that are well run have a better succession plan. I think with the family-owned, it's super complicated because one thing is what does the founder want? But it's also, well, what does the next generation want? And the fact is that while business is dynamic, and it's impacted by things you can control, but oftentimes things you can't control like the economy, industry, competition, etc. Families are impacted that way too. And families change and grow. Next generation tends to get married to other people, which brings other people into the mix, etc. And so, all of these things make it very complicated. It's certainly a best practice to write some things down. We would agree with that. But what is written down and the flexibility around what is written down to be able to adapt to new circumstances and things that come down the pike is vitally important. And so, having a plan is a really good thing from a structure standpoint. But it's also a really good thing to make sure there is flexibility built in to allow for things that will inevitably occur. FX de Mallmann: I wanted to just pick up on your question, Allison. In my experience, many of these founder owners tend initially, certainly in their lifetime, to be extremely busy, extremely preoccupied and engaged in their business. And often prioritize their business over long-term planning. Often this is for the right reason to the great benefit of the business. And then the second key factor is orchestrating and considering this decision forces some pretty hard judgments, some of which they're able to do at a certain point in time, some of which they'd rather have more time to consider, including is their family, are their children capable? Do they have the relevant experience or desire to be involved in the business? Some cases it's too early to judge. Many of these founders decide that taking more time and having more visibility with the passage of time will de-risk some of these decisions. Allison Nathan: And as you said, FX, it's a process. Because you have these creators, they're focused on growing their business. But at some point, they do transition to thinking about how the business is going to outlive them. So, what does that transition look like, especially for families that do this well? FX de Mallmann: That process really involves facing those two questions. Should my family, any family members be involved in the business itself in a management role, junior or senior, but over time, senior, yes or no? And how do I organize the ownership to be transferred from one generation to the other? On the first one, my own view is it's a very delicate judgment, but really relies on is there someone who is capable, who has the relevant experience, and who has a desire to rise up to the occasion. That judgment needs to be as independent as possible. Typically, the founder is the absolute best person to render that judgment. In some cases, we see them soliciting external input to benchmark or compare their own family members with external talent. And what we find on average is the larger the company, the more global, the more complex, typically, the more likely it will require a non-family member with significant experience to continue to run it. And we see many family businesses choosing to bring professional management as they scale up. On the second, which is a question of how does the ownership get passed on, the initial typical approach is to say, let's divide the ownership equally between the number of children or sort of second-generation family members. The question that brings is, what's the organization of that group? How large is that group? Has any member got the right to exit if she wants to or he wants to? And what's the mechanism to exit? And how do any conflicts get tackled and resolved? Is this within the family or is this with a governance structure that allows the resolution of conflict? And in my experience, this process and this mechanism needs to be thought through early on before the number of family members gets too large. And typically, having some exit right of some form and having some conflict resolution mechanism in case there is one or disagreement on any point goes a long way. Allison Nathan: And as we touched on, it's not necessarily just about the family dynamics. There's a whole world, there's an economic cycle, because ultimately, they can pass on and keep the business in the family. But there's also the ability to IPO. There's the ability to sell outright. So, how big of a driver are these other factors when you're talking to families as they work through this? FX de Mallmann: In many cases, one of the questions the companies face, and the family faces is, does the company need external capital to scale the business? And typically, when there is a capital need, it brings the question of who are the investors, what's the source of capital, and by how much should the family get diluted as part of that? That's one big aspect. A second aspect, and we've seen numerous examples of this, is a number of families decide and believe that bringing a third-party investor, whether it's a single investor or a group of investors, and it could also be the public market, can be a source of discipline and a forcing mechanism around many aspects that may be complicated to discuss or resolved within the family. Some choose to sell either because they believe it's the right thing for their business or the right thing for the family. What I have witnessed many times in the context of the sale is there could be great economic outcomes and great solutions for businesses to be consolidated, merged or sold, but that often the family has part of its identity in the business and a sale has a significant impact on the family's emotions and on their sense of identity that's tied to the business. Tucker York: Allison, just to tack on to that from FX both expertise, but also, if you will, the objective is to take care of the health and well-being of the business. In doing that, he's interacting directly with the founder/CEO. It's a different element about, I'll call it, the health and well-being of the family and what's in their best interest. And sometimes it's aligned and sometimes it's not. I think the other thing, too, for any succession planning or any long-term capital structure planning, that also changes over time. And so, this concept of we're going to make a plan and then we're good, it doesn't apply. It needs to be reviewed and stress-tested regularly. In the same way, as you think about next generation planning, most parents, when they think about their children, it's a different set of circumstances when they're 35 than when they're five, and how to think about that. And so, again, it's a regular review of where we are in the process. FX de Mallmann: Tucker, I think you raise just an excellent point on this, which is typically in the first generation, the interests of the business are very aligned and mirror the interests of the family. If it's one individual, it's his business. That's his life or her life. FX de Mallmann: As a number of generations passes, the family's interests may differ from the business interest, and being very clear on whether that's the case, where do they align and where do they differ, is step number one in long-term planning. Tucker York: On the same line, that founder is the shareholder. And so, what they want to do for the business and what they want to do for their wealth creation is the same. And many founders say, "One of the things I want to do with this is I want to give this business to the next generation." There are other founders who say, "What I want to do is I want to give the advantages that I have to the next generation, but I want them to do something different or whatever they want, or etc." And all of those things, again, as that next generation grows, the complexity around that grows as well. Allison Nathan: So, that gets to the wealth creation aspect of this, Tucker, which you have a lot of insight into. Because ultimately, the day a founder sells the company or takes it public, they end up with wealth. And it basically becomes like this pile of money that they have never had to manage before, versus a business that they were managing day in and day out. How do the largest families navigate this and handle this? Tucker York: Well, it's not necessarily what they started out for, but it is an outcome of the success they have and how they think about that, how they think about the way an endowment would think about its money. What is this money for? What is its purpose? What are the other, not only wealth that I want to pass along, but what are the values I want to pass along? And all of that comes into the thing. And yes, so the mindset does change over time. Allison Nathan: And not just the mindset, the organizational structure, the resources required to manage this wealth that is now outside the business versus in the business changes. Tucker York: For sure. And I think it's varied how that works. Some people say, "Well, I want to set up now a new business whose job it is to manage the wealth that I created." Others would say, "I don't aspire to be in that business. I realize that I have to 'take care of these resources in a different way than when it was all in the business'" and they go in different routes. And the reality is, this is what's very interesting about the roles that we get to play is it runs the range. There isn't everybody does it this way or that way. They think about different things. And again, that's where family comes into play as well. FX de Mallmann: Allison, if I just can add one thing on this, we're also seeing in this process, often important differences between first generation family members who involve the business and who often have limited time or choose to spend limited time on allocating or managing the capital that's outside the business. Versus the second generation and onwards who inherit a lot of wealth and a lot of capital and who's one of the important projects, but also responsibilities, is to be good stewards of this capital. And Tucker and his team have a lot of experience with the dynamic between the first generation, the second generation, and the amount of time and effort and resources that each individual family members or branches choose to or want to spend in managing their own assets. Allison Nathan: We end this conversation how we began it with this long-term mindset that these families have, but to your point, Tucker, with some flexibility so they can adapt to the changing family and business dynamics. But in some ways, my takeaway is in a way, as we talked to our individual investors, people potentially listening to this podcast, there is always an emphasis on long-term planning for your own wealth. That those who plan and think about this succession ultimately end up in a better spot than those who don't. Is that a takeaway here about thinking about always having that long-term plan in your mind? Tucker York: I think it absolutely is. People say long-term oriented, that's a better way to be. But if you take a step back, we live in an incredibly short-term oriented world. And so, it's hard to push against that. The way money is managed, it's nice to be able to see your stock that you own go up and down in price. But if it goes up a lot, you're tempted to sell, then you pay taxes, and you have to figure out what to do with it again. If you're in a private company or a private equity, you're holding it for a longer period of time, but then you don't have the flexibility if you need the money to do this thing. What I would argue is it leans towards people should be thinking about staying consistently invested. And a safer way to do that is to not just own one thing, but to own a portfolio of things. So, that on average, the market goes higher over a period of time if you believe in global GDP growth. But that to me is the takeaway. These extraordinary families that have built the enterprises that FX deals with regularly, they have made concentrated bets in one, basically, company that becomes a stock. And that's a way for tremendous wealth creation. But it's incredibly risky. And the things that we don't talk about on podcasts like that are the many other people who tried that and it didn't work. And so, again, you blend the two together. It's owning equity, but doing it in a diversified way and staying consistently long or invested. Allison Nathan: FX, anything to add in terms of a closing message? FX de Mallmann: I fully agree. And what we've seen is many of these entrepreneurs that have created extraordinary businesses have played the long game. They have deployed capital, they have adjusted and adapted their business and investment decisions through many cycles, including volatile times, but they remain invested. And many of those and many families that have benefited from this, it's not only to remain invested, but to continue to invest, whether it's adding capital, buying back stock in the market in their own businesses through the cycle to increase their ownership. So, these are very concentrated bets. But when you have very disciplined, long-term stewards of capital that know and understand the business and are able to attract and retain great management and make disciplined decisions with respect to their family ownership, you typically have a winning recipe for great success and great value creation. JPMorgan Chase (NYSE:JPM | JPM Price Prediction) or Goldman Sachs (NYSE:GS): which megabank should a retirement-focused income investor own right now? JPMorgan pays $1.65 a quarter today, and Goldman pays $5.00. The more revealing number comes from 2009, when JPMorgan cut its quarterly dividend to $0.05. Goldman kept paying $0.35 straight through the crisis. The bank with the strong reputation cut. The bank known for risk-taking held. JPMorgan lifted its quarterly payout to $1.65 from $1.50, a forward annual rate of $6.60. Trailing 12-month dividends total $6.00. Goldman raised its payout 11% to $5.00 from $4.50, a forward rate of $20.00 after $18.00 over the trailing year. Management says that dividend is up 25% versus a year ago and 150% over the last five years. Per-share size misleads readers constantly. Yield equals the dividend divided by the share price, and Goldman trades at $911.25 against JPMorgan’s $335.34. On trailing payouts, Goldman yields 1.84% versus 1.77% for JPMorgan. That gap is thin. Both are dividend growers with modest current yields. Winner: Goldman, on the pace of its raises. JPMorgan’s quarterly dividend stood at $0.38 at the January 2, 2009 ex-dividend date. From the April 2, 2009 ex-date, it paid $0.05 and held that low level for roughly two years before rebuilding. Goldman paid $0.35 per quarter across every ex-dividend date from 2008 through 2011. A retiree living on JPMorgan checks watched income shrink to a nickel. A Goldman holder saw no break (the warning signs before a cut like that are the subject of a free report we put together on dividend traps). Winner: Goldman. Context matters. JPMorgan is a deposit-funded universal bank under far greater regulation, and the pressure it faced in 2009 differed in kind from Goldman’s. Today both banks run through the Federal Reserve’s annual stress test. Regulators model a severe recession, set a stress capital buffer, and dividends plus buybacks must fit above the resulting minimum. Earnings matter, but capital ratios set the ceiling on payouts. The 2009 record is evidence, and today’s regime determines the next test. Many successful investors eventually reach the same moment. The saving is done, the portfolio is built, and the question quietly changes from how much can I grow this to how much can I take out? Goldman’s was 12.9% against an 11.4% requirement, a 150 basis point cushion, with a 3.4% stress capital buffer through September of 2027. Goldman also swings harder. Its beta is 1.283 versus 0.975 for JPMorgan, and over the past month Goldman fell 11.43% while JPMorgan slipped 6.23%. Goldman’s second-quarter net income jumped 78.03% on a capital markets surge, while JPMorgan’s adjusted EPS of $6.14 rose 13%. Jamie Dimon, CEO at the time of the July call, warned: “It’s getting close to as good as it gets. We just don’t know how long it’s going to last.” Goldman’s earnings ride that cycle more directly. Winner: JPMorgan. For an income investor, Goldman takes it. It yields slightly more, raises faster, trades at a forward P/E of 13 versus 14 for JPMorgan, and has the cleaner crisis record. JPMorgan fits the retiree whose top priority is a smaller drawdown in a selloff, since its lower beta and deeper capital buffer deliver exactly that. The development that would flip the call: Goldman’s cushion over its capital requirement. title: The Suzuki Adventure Bike That Rivals The BMW GS At A Lower Price - Top Speed
content: Subscribe to the TopSpeed newsletter to never miss an update The adventure bike segment has never been more competitive, yet one name continues to cast a long shadow over every rival: the BMW GS. BMW essentially invented the adventure bike category with the R 80 G/S in the early 1980s, and the GS lineage has carried that benchmark status ever since. The problem? BMW has never been known for keeping prices reasonable. Even the middleweight F 900 GS carries a starting price that climbs well past $14,000 in base trim — and that's before you start ticking option boxes. The good news is that you don't need a German budget to live out your adventure fantasies. Suzuki's V-Strom 800DE makes a compelling case for itself in the middleweight ADV class: a Dakar-inspired machine that pairs Japanese reliability with genuine off-road capability, all at a price that significantly undercuts the BMW. It strikes a near-perfect balance of everyday usability, long-haul comfort, and go-anywhere confidence — without the premium price tag. Here's why the V-Strom 800DE deserves a serious look. Within Suzuki's V-Strom lineup, the V-Strom 800DE is the most off-road-focused model in the family — equally at home on the daily commute and a cross-continental journey. It is powered by a tractable parallel-twin engine, complemented by fully adjustable Showa suspension and long-distance ergonomics. Wrapped in a Dakar-inspired design, the V-Strom can be yours for well under $12,000. That bang-for-buck appeal is only reinforced by Suzuki's well-earned reputation for low running costs and long-term reliability. The BMW F 900 GS, by comparison, starts at over $14,000. That's not to say the V-Strom is perfect, though. The value-focused formula does come with trade-offs. It doesn't produce nearly as much power or torque as the BMW F 900 GS, nor is it among the lightest bikes in the class. It also misses out on some notable features, including cruise control, tubeless tires, and radial-mount brake calipers — which is partly why it's often overlooked in the segment. Look past those shortcomings, however, and you'll find a terrific adventure bike that covers everything you'd actually need your ADV to do, without breaking the bank. Unlike the V-Strom 650 and 1050, the V-Strom 800 uses a parallel-twin engine shared with the GSX-8R and GSX-8S — a pairing that speaks to the motor's versatile character. According to Suzuki, the engine is tuned for smooth, controllable low-end torque while still revving freely to its peak power output. It produces just over 80 horsepower, which is more than sufficient for everyday riding, off-road excursions, and long-distance touring, even if it falls short of the F 900 GS on paper. The absence of a V-twin may give some traditional V-Strom fans pause, but in practice you're not missing much. The engine retains a V-twin-like character courtesy of its 270-degree firing order. It's also notable as the first Suzuki production motorcycle to feature a cross balancer, which enables a more compact, lightweight layout. The result is a powerplant that occupies less space than a V-twin while delivering similar power pulses that enhance traction and strong low-rpm tractability. Parallel-twin, 270-degree crankshaft, DOHC, liquid-cooled Suzuki says the engine is also tuned for good fuel economy, and according to its UK website, it returns just over 53 US MPG in combined conditions. That's respectable efficiency for a do-it-all ADV, and with the 5.3-gallon fuel tank, you can expect a range of over 280 miles between fuel stops. The Suzuki Clutch Assist System (SCAS) and a bidirectional quickshifter round out the package, making gear changes smoother whether you're filtering through city traffic or cruising the highway. The V-Strom 800DE is the most off-road-capable V-Strom currently on sale, and that's where it closes the gap with the F 900 GS most convincingly. It's built around a steel backbone frame tuned for straight-line stability and nimble handling. According to Suzuki, the chassis keeps the bike composed on the highway while remaining easy to thread through trails and forest roads. The one notable downside is a curb weight of over 500 pounds — on the heavier side for the segment. The frame is paired with Showa suspension designed to deliver comfort and performance across all surfaces. Full adjustability gives riders the freedom to dial in behavior to suit their style and load. With 8.7 inches of travel at both ends and the highest ground clearance in the V-Strom family, the 800DE inspires the confidence to tackle obstacles without scraping the engine cases. Showa Linkage-type monoshock, fully adjustable, 8.7 in. travel Dual 310mm discs with Nissin two-piston floating calipers A 21-inch front spoke wheel makes the V-Strom 800DE even more off-road capable, providing better stability on trails and a smoother ride on broken pavement. The 17-inch rear spoke wheel handles grip and comfort at the back. Both wheels are shod in Dunlop Trailmax Mixtour tires with a semi-block pattern that balances off- and on-road traction. Braking duties are handled by a pair of Nissin axial-mount calipers up front and a single unit at the rear. One look at the V-Strom 800DE and its new-generation Suzuki identity is unmistakable — the aggressive, mass-forward design is sharp and contemporary, and it looks particularly striking in the Champion Yellow No. 2 colorway. The Glass Sparkle Black option is equally appealing for those who prefer a more understated look. Either way, Suzuki says the modern styling draws inspiration from the legendary DR-Z Dakar racer and the DR-Big dual sport, with a focus on long-distance comfort and off-road ease. The wide, tapered handlebar is cast in strong yet flexible aluminum, allowing it to absorb shock during off-road riding. The wider grips are designed to remain comfortable in a variety of conditions, including when standing on the pegs. Speaking of which, the footpegs are broad and fitted with vibration-dampening rubber inserts that can be removed for extra grip on the trails. Suzuki says the seat is both supportive and narrow, keeping it comfortable over long distances while remaining accessible for a wide range of rider heights. The front cowl and windscreen are wind-tunnel tested to reduce buffeting on the rider while maximizing visibility from the saddle. The windshield is adjustable across three positions, though you'll need a hex tool to undo and redo the four screws each time. That's a genuine miss on Suzuki's part — most rivals offer tool-free windscreen adjustment. On the plus side, the clutch and brake levers can be adjusted without any tools at all. The V-Strom 800DE's electronics suite is where the bike's budget-conscious nature is most apparent. The package centers on a 5-inch TFT display — smaller than what the F 900 GS offers — and the Suzuki Intelligent Ride System (S.I.R.S.), which bundles traction control, rider modes, a quickshifter, easy start, and low RPM assist. Notably absent are a six-axis IMU and cruise control, even as optional extras. Suzuki partially compensates with a solid range of Genuine Suzuki Accessories, including side and top cases, an engine guard, center stand, low and high seat options, heated grips, and auxiliary lamps. There's also the V-Strom 800DE Adventure variant, which adds a durable aluminum bash plate and aluminum panniers as standard equipment. For context, the BMW F 900 GS offers a more extensive optional extras catalog, including Keyless Ride, TPMS, Sport suspension, a high windscreen, the BMW Motorrad ConnectedRide Navigator, and more. It's clear that the V-Strom 800DE is a more straightforward package than the BMW GS — but holding that against it misses the point entirely. The V-Strom isn't trying to dazzle you with outright performance or a long features list. Instead, it's built to nail the fundamentals of a middleweight adventure bike: friendly power delivery, long-distance comfort, genuine off-road ability, and essential rider aids. It's a solid ADV that gives you everything you actually need, without charging you for the bells and whistles you may never use. We want to hear from you. While he didn’t struggle, he ended the season without a flourish or without hitting some favorable benchmarks (ERA under 3.00, 200+ strikeouts), and as such, I think that ship has sailed. Regardless, McLean’s 2026 was a total success in just about every measure, with the right-hander being well above-average all year except for a stretch in May. McLean might not be the best pitcher in baseball, but the Mets certainly have their ace. Who would’ve foreseen this back in April, when he was struggling? His 118 wRC+ and 4.1 fWAR/4.2 rWAR are the most by a Mets rookie since Pete Alonso’s 2019 Rookie of the Year season. Then, he had a brief cup of coffee at the end of the season, and things have been all awry since then. It was reported that the Mets altered his arm slot, lowering it to ensure that, in the words of Eric Jaegers, it did not “tak[e] away from some other things”- meaning his secondary pitches- and sought to “diversify [his] arsenal” by adding a new cutter grip to his repertoire. I don’t remember where I read the tagline, but on the matter, somebody wrote something along the lines of “Jonah Tong is being reshaped to fit the Mets’ vision” rather than developed as what he already is. His fastball lost a few crucial inches of induced vertical break and became less effective. His new cutter was brutalized by Triple-A hitters. His command took a step back as compared to prior years. None of this is to say that Jonah Tong was perfect prior to the 2026 season, but the right-hander struggled for most of the year, and a lot of that seems to have been self-inflicted by the organization. He looked better towards the end of the season and ended things on a high note in his last game of the season against Washington, so here’s hoping that Tong learns from everything he went through this season and comes back in 2027 a better pitcher. Two days later, on May 12, he drove in a run with an RBI triple off of Enmanual De Jesus, having already drawn three walks, in a Mets 10-2 blowout of the Detroit Tigers. It feels crazy now, but five months ago, AJ Ewing was still in Double-A. The 21-year-old has not been as consistent as his fellow rookie outfielder Carson Benge and is still much more a work-in-progress, but there’s a very good chance the team has found its long-term centerfielder. He struggled early in the season and then missed most of June and all of July due to separate groin and hip injuries. He returned to the field in August healthy and posted numbers that are more like Jacob Reimer, but he fell apart once again at the end of the season. Since being drafted in 2022, the infielder’s career has felt like a see-saw: one year he’ll be good, then he’ll have a down year due to injuries, then he’ll recover and be good, then he’ll have a down year due to injuries. Despite 512 at-bats under his belt at the Double-A level split between 2025 and 2026 and a cumulative .252/.352/.424 batting line to show for it, I would assume that the 22-year-old is a lock to be added to the 40-man roster to protect him from the 2026 Rule 5 Draft (if that even takes place). Here’s hoping that 2027 will be an upswing year for him.
